hints: Start by thinking what a base must do with its nitrogen lone pair, then compare how free that lone pair is in an amide, an aromatic amine and an aliphatic amine.

Look at what is directly attached to nitrogen in each compound, a $\text{C=O}$ group, a benzene ring, or a $\text{CH}_2$ group, and decide if it pulls electrons away or pushes electrons towards nitrogen.
Link delocalisation into the ring in T and delocalisation onto oxygen in S to reduced availability of the lone pair, compared with the localised lone pair in U.
walkthrough:
Picture basicity as lone pair availability**
Think of basicity in a very concrete way. A base uses a lone pair on nitrogen to pick up an $\text{H}^+$ ion. So the question becomes, in which molecule is the lone pair most free and most electron rich? Draw the three structures in your mind: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.

Compare U with T, why the CH2 spacer matters**
In T, phenylamine, the nitrogen is attached directly to the benzene ring. Its lone pair can overlap with the delocalised pi electrons of the ring and is pulled partly into the ring. That makes it less ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$. In U, phenylmethanamine, there is a $\text{CH}_2$ group between the ring and the $\text{NH}_2$. That spacer stops any overlap with the ring, so the lone pair stays localised on nitrogen. The alkyl group also pushes electrons towards nitrogen, making the lone pair even more ready to accept a proton. So U is more basic than T.

See why the amide S is essentially neutral**
In S, benzamide, nitrogen is next to a $\text{C=O}$ group. Oxygen is very electronegative and the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen. You can think of it as being tied up in the amide bond. There is almost no free lone pair left to accept $\text{H}^+$. That is why amides are neutral and far less basic than amines. Putting it together gives $\text{U > T > S}$.

Final answer: U most basic > T > S least basic
U, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, is most basic as the alkyl $\text{CH}_2$ group is electron donating, so the nitrogen lone pair is readily available to accept a proton.
T, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, is less basic as the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the delocalised pi system of the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.
S, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$, is least basic / neutral as the electron withdrawing carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ group withdraws the lone pair, so it is not available to accept a proton.

hints: For reaction 1, count oxygens: the $\text{C=O}$ of the amide becomes $\text{CH}_2$ in the amine, so oxygen is lost and hydrogen is gained. Recall which hydride reagent is strong enough for amides.
For reaction 2, the $\text{Br}$ atom is replaced by $\text{NH}_2$. Think what nitrogen nucleophile supplies this and what conditions prevent further substitution and drive the reaction.
walkthrough:
Recognise reaction 1 as amide to amine**
Look at the change: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The carbonyl oxygen is removed and hydrogens are added. This is reduction of an amide. The usual mild hydride $\text{NaBH}_4$ cannot do this. You need the powerful reducing agent $\text{LiAlH}_4$, usually in dry ether followed by acid work up.

Recognise reaction 2 as bromoalkane to amine**
Here $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ becomes $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Bromine is replaced by $\text{NH}_2$. The nucleophile is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$. To favour the primary amine product and force substitution, use excess ammonia heated under pressure or in a sealed tube.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{LiAlH}_4$
reaction 2: heat $\text{NH}_3$ under pressure / heat $\text{NH}_3$ in a sealed tube / excess hot $\text{NH}_3$

hints: For reaction 1, focus on the change in oxygen and hydrogen content at carbon to decide if it is oxidation, reduction or substitution.
For reaction 2, focus on how $\text{NH}_3$ attacks carbon and what happens to $\text{Br}$, recalling the name of that bond breaking and bond making pattern for halogenoalkanes.
walkthrough:
Classify reaction 1**
The amide carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ loses oxygen and gains hydrogen to give $\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Gain of hydrogen and loss of oxygen is reduction, so reaction 1 is a reduction.

Name the mechanism of reaction 2**
Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, has a lone pair and acts as a nucleophile attacking the electron deficient carbon attached to $\text{Br}$. Bromide leaves as $\text{Br}^-$. One nucleophile replaces one leaving group in a single step, so the mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

Final answer: type of reaction in reaction 1: reduction
mechanism of reaction 2: nucleophilic substitution
